newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch closing share market report.
newsitem.headline: Dutch closing share market report.

text.p: Dutch shares ended well down as the market turned bearish on EMU worries with Wall Street's opening slump driving the AEX further down in closing trade.
Dutch blue chips ended down almost across the board, with the AEX finishing 13.65 points or 1.70 percent lower at 790.97.
The index opened off a touch at 804.92, with private demand ensuring losses stayed limited. But they soon started to slide as professionals took their cue from lower surrounding bourses.
Dealers had initially expected the AEX to stay above 800 points, but once this apparent support fell away, the way was opened for a fall towards key support at around 780.
"The 800 level did not constitute real support, but the fact the index fell through was generally considered a bad signal," one dealer said.
He said most institutional players had chosen to exit the market, with late trade consisting mainly of share baskets reflecting options-led index-related activity.
"Institutions will wait and see what happens (in the second round of French elections) on Sunday," another dealer added.
Prospects of a Socialist win in France and protracted wrangling over German plans to revalue gold reserves have kindled worries about the future of European Monetary Union.
Consequently sentiment in Amsterdam -- as on other markets -- turned bearish and worsened in the wake of Wall Street's opening slump as hi-techs tumbled on Intel's profit warning.
Nevertheless the AEX closed back from the day's low of 788.06.
"What happens on Monday depends on the French election outcome and Wall Street's close," one dealer said.
Others agreed, saying dual listings of major Dutch stocks such as ABN Amro and Ahold meant Amsterdam's performance was tracking that of New York ever more closely.
Light profit-taking in financials also undermined the index.
Financial services group ING, which on Thursday posted first-quarter results up 21 percent, fell two guilders to 84.90, while ABN Amro lost 0.50 to 35.50 guilders.
Dealers said that investors were inclined to take profits now that financials appeared to be pausing in their protracted march ahead.

One of the biggest blue chip losers was chemicals group Akzo Nobel, which shed a hefty 12.70 guilders in brisk trade to 255.70. Dealers said the drop reflected analysts' disappointment at the lack of hard figures to relieve doubts about the profit slowdown at Akzo's pharmaceuticals activities.
By contrast an upbeat presentation to analysts in London from retail giant Ahold braked the shares' fall in a depressed market.
Ahold shares dipped 0.50 guilders to 145.90, a loss of just 0.34 percent.
